Point estimate and 90% credible interval, per component
log scale · MWp · hover a row for detail
Each row is one addend of the Best estimate; the top row is their sum. The intervals do not add up to the total's: components that share an error source were drawn together (one area-to-capacity constant for every rooftop figure, one for every ground-mount figure, one re-draw of the calibration areas for every roofclf figure), so the total's interval is narrower than the sum of the parts' intervals would suggest. A row without a whisker is a deterministic correction rather than a modelled quantity. The intervals cover measured errors only; "How confident should you be in this?" below lists what they leave out.

    What is PV glint and how is it detected?

    PV Glint is a brief, brighter-than-diffuse flash where a panel's specular reflection lines up with the sun and Sentinel-2's fixed overpass geometry on one date -- see the method page for the full derivation and an annotated image gallery. A single spike can't be checked for self-consistency -- 0% of installations glint once (or on dates that disagree on a panel geometry) and so are correctly detected as "PV is probably here" but carry no orientation information.

    Why the plot only fills part of the circle

    Sentinel-2 crosses this latitude at a fixed ~10:30 local time, so in every image of the survey window the sun's azimuth at the moment of overpass never once swings west of due south -- a panel facing southwest, west, or north cannot glint into this sensor no matter how long you wait. That's a sensor limit, not a property of rooftops here: the shaded wedge (0° wide) marks orientations this survey cannot observe at all, not orientations known to be empty. Nothing is plotted there, because nothing was measured there.

    Data: . Validated = a single (tilt, azimuth) explains ≥ 2 independent spike dates via the specular reflection condition, tolerance 3°. Point size ∝ √(installation area). Hover a point to see which installation it is; click it to open that installation in OpenStreetMap. The CSV download lists every point with its OSM id and coordinates. Full derivation of the glint signal this pose fit is built on: the method page. Annotated Sentinel-2 / high-res examples of what a validated spike actually looks like in the source imagery: the image gallery.

    Background
    How to read these numbers
    How the estimate is built the methods in plain language, what each can see, how they add up+
    How confident should you be in this? preliminary results, sampling caveats, independent corroboration+

    Best estimate: 41,777 MWp, with a 90% range of 37,232–56,235 MWp. The range covers two measured sources of uncertainty, not everything that could move this number. Below: what is inside the range, and what is not.

    Inside the range:

    • The two area-to-power constants. Panel area on a roof converts at about 0.18 kWp per m², the rating of a typical module; the outline of a ground-mounted park converts at about 0.05 kWp per m², measured on parks whose capacity is known. Each is varied over its own range (90%: 0.15–0.21 and 0.035–0.075 kWp per m²).
    • How reliable the segmentation model's detections are. How often its detections turn out to be real, and how many mapped arrays it misses, were measured size class by size class against mapped installations. Those measurements have their own sampling error, which is drawn into the range.

    Outside the range, and not something more arithmetic can add back:

    • No area of this country has been exhaustively mapped by hand to check these numbers against. The detectors' measured accuracy is carried over from the countries where it was measured, and how well it transfers here has not itself been measured. That is a different kind of uncertainty from the range above, and no amount of arithmetic converts one into the other.
    • The small-installation half of this page does not exist yet. No area of Spain has been mapped panel by panel, so there is nothing to calibrate a per-building rooftop classifier against here. Everything on the map is either hand-mapped in OpenStreetMap or an array the segmentation model outlined directly, which in practice means installations of roughly 400 m² and up. Household and small-business rooftop systems are mostly below that size.
    • Concentrated solar plants are counted, but not as photovoltaics. Spain's parabolic-trough and tower plants are tagged in OpenStreetMap much like solar parks. They were taken out before training and out of the photovoltaic layers, and each plant counts in Best and Verified at its electric rating, not by its mirror area.
    • Nearly every cell was imaged. Map cells were imaged if they hold at least one known building or any hand-mapped solar installation, a wider net than most countries on this site. Cells that hold neither are hatched on the map: they were not looked at, which is not the same as holding no solar.
    • Building footprints are stitched from two sources. The open footprint dataset used elsewhere (VIDA) has large gaps in Spain, including the centres of Seville, Valencia and Málaga. Those gaps were filled with OpenStreetMap buildings, which are themselves incomplete in places, so rooftop and ground placement and the choice of which cells to image are less even here than the map suggests.
    • Very large model outlines count only once checked. A model outline above 100,000 m² counts only when it is mapped or a person has judged it solar, which removes large false detections and, with them, any real park nobody has looked at yet. Spain's have not been judged yet, so the real parks among them are still missing from Best. Mapping such a park brings it into the verified layer.
    • On open ground, most of what the model adds is not solar. Looked at on imagery, the largest unmapped outlines in the cells where Best most exceeds Verified are mostly bare rock outcrops in the western woodlands, arable fields and quarries, with some real parks among them. Such outlines reach Best at the mapped share of their size class, which is high for large ground outlines because Spain's solar parks are so well mapped. Verified, which counts only mapped installations, is not affected.
    • The plausibility check cannot vouch for the regional figures here. It compares each region's ground-mounted capacity with its rooftop capacity, and nearly every Spanish region fails or is flagged. That is expected where rooftop systems are mostly too small for the model to see, since the comparison then has almost nothing to divide by. It also means the check says little either way about false detections on open ground.

    Treat this as an early estimate from an active research pipeline, not a census. What it offers is a reproducible way to estimate distributed solar from free satellite imagery and open-source models where official statistics are thin or missing. Expect the figures to move as the evidence behind them grows.

    Nothing on this page rests on hand-mapped ground truth from this country. Exhaustively mapped areas -- every panel in a few square kilometres, drawn by hand -- are what turns a detection into a capacity estimate: they measure how much of a flagged roof is actually covered in panels, and how many real installations the detectors miss entirely. Until some exist here, read these figures accordingly. Mapping one is the most useful thing anyone can contribute.

    Using the map and exporting figures layers, your own data, downloads, licences+

    Layers. "Show" picks the quantity the cells are coloured by: the Best estimate, the OSM-mapped capacity alone, the satellite detections above 400 m², rooftop PV below it, farm ground PV below it (arrays beside fields, where the farm detector has run), or the gap between the Best estimate and what is already mapped, which is where mapping effort pays off most. Each cell shows its total in MWp. The colour scale is logarithmic and is refitted to whichever quantity is shown; the legend always states its range.

    Your own data. "Layers" → "Add a layer" overlays a GeoJSON file, a CSV with latitude/longitude columns, a GeoJSON URL, an XYZ raster tile URL or a WMS (use {bbox-epsg-3857} in its GetMap URL). Files are read in your browser and are not uploaded anywhere. The live OpenStreetMap overlay queries the public Overpass API for the area in view when you zoom in, so it shows mapping done after this page was built.

    Exports. Every figure downloads as PNG (for slides), SVG (vector, for papers) and CSV (the numbers behind it); the map as PNG with its legend and attribution, and the grid as GeoJSON or CSV. Basemap imagery and tiles keep their own providers' terms: OpenStreetMap data is © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), the grey canvas and the satellite imagery © Esri and its partners.

    Read more on the project's documentation site: capacity methodology · roofclf · farm ground PV · Sentinel-2 glint & panel pose · calibration quadrats · experiment register.

The raw-detections download above predates this page and will go stale as mappers keep editing; this query always reflects live OSM state.
    Capacity data

    The capacity per grid cell shown on the map, as CSV. One row per 0.1° cell, generated in your browser from the data this page is drawing, so it is exactly the numbers above. lon0/lat0 are the south-west corner of the cell. The GeoParquet carries the cell polygon in EPSG:4326, so it opens directly in QGIS or GeoPandas.
